newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission says forest damage increasing.
newsitem.headline: Commission says forest damage increasing.

text.p: Forest damage is increasing in Europe, according to the annual Forest Condition in Europe report issued by the European Commission on Thursday.

"The results of the 1995 survey show that almost one in five trees in the European Union (18.1 percent of the sample) has clear signs of damage (over 25 percent defoliation)," the Commission said in a statement.

The survey on which the 1996 Forest Report is based was carried out in the 15 member states of the EU and 15 other European countries by the European Commission and the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe.
"Although improvements of forest condition were reported from certain locations the overall forest damage seems to increase on the European level," the report said.
Drought and heat had a particularly high impact on forests together with pest infection and the actions of man. Game and grazing also impaired the forests studied.
Direct and indirect effects of air pollution caused serious decline in some areas particularly in central Europe.

The report says that only in a few cases studied had air pollution been identified as a cause of damge but other sources of information suggest that it may cause trees to decline over much wider areas although this remains uncertain.

"While sulphur deposition has been drastically reduced in comparison with the seventies, nitrogen deposition from different sources is still high impairing soil chemistry and foliar nutrient status in some areas," the report said.
The Commission is coordinating an intensive forest-ecosystem monitoring programme to complement the annual forest surveys.
